title: Iran ramps up attacks on Gulf countries after U.S. strikes
rawText:
Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp up tit-for-tat strikes
What to know about the Iran war:
- Bahrain and Kuwait said Wednesday that they intercepted weapons launched by Iran after the U.S. carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran appears to be stepping up attacks on America's Persian Gulf allies as tension ratchets back up across the region.
- A U.S. official called the Tuesday strikes on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island a defensive response to Iranian forces "targeting U.S. personnel and assets" in the region. The strikes came hours after Iran said it targeted a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain for the third time in less than a week. Those attacks were all intercepted, U.S. authorities said.
- A crew member was missing Wednesday after a ship belonging to the United Arab Emirates' state oil company ADNOC was struck in the Strait of Hormuz, the energy firm said. Eleven people were injured, and search and rescue operations were ongoing, according to ADNOC.
Mideast crisis "largest threat" to energy security ever, world energy body says
The crisis in the Middle East sparked in February by the U.S and Israel bombing Iran has created the "largest threat" to energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned Thursday.
The agency said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies.
The crisis, just like previous energy shocks, would certainly leave "lasting marks", the agency warned.
Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area.
Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through vital channel — which before the war carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments — supply lines remain severely disrupted.
"The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report.
He highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, and China buying less from international markets.
"Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply," Birol wrote.
The report said that "increasingly it is falling to consumers -- and high prices -- to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down".
Birol had struck a more positive tone in July, when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from "several cushioning factors."
Saudi skyscraper damaged in Riyad, witnesses say
A skyscraper in Riyadh that houses the headquarters of the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund was damaged on Thursday, witnesses told AFP, following weeks of attacks on the kingdom by Yemen's Houthis rebels.
"The facade is damaged across several floors, with windows blown out," a source who requested anonymity told AFP. Two other sources confirmed the damage to the building, which has 80 floors and is the tallest tower in the Saudi capital's financial district.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis had said earlier that it had handled a missile threat launched by the militia toward Riyadh and that an early assessment was that debris had fallen and there was material damage, according to the Reuters news service.

title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
rawText:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.
“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.
He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.
In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.
Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.
“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

title: Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
rawText:
Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
The artificial intelligence company Anthropic said on Wednesday it sold more than 956 million shares at a price of $83 a piece in a record-breaking initial public offering that makes it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
The five-year-old AI powerhouse raised around $79.4 billion through the offering, exceeding the $75 billion IPO haul of Elon Musk's SpaceX earlier this year. Anthropic said in a statement that "certain stockholders" also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO, bringing the total haul to more than $81.3 billion.
Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
The listing was oversubscribed, despite coming at a time of growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.
The number of shares sold and the price exceeded Anthropic's original expectations. The listing prospectus targeted a sale of 825 million shares at $70 to $78 per share.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

title: Hegseth alardea de la captura de Maduro en la primera visita a Venezuela de un secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. en décadas
rawText:
Hegseth alardea de la captura de Maduro en la primera visita a Venezuela de un secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. en décadas
  - Autor, Redacción
  - Título del autor, BBC News Mundo
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 3 min
"Hoy hace exactamente un año, el imputado fugitivo narcoterrorista Nicolás Maduro, el hombre que pasó más de una década entregándoles las fronteras y el territorio de Venezuela a terroristas de todas partes del mundo, se paró en un escenario no muy lejos de aquí y gritó en tono de burla: 'Vengan y agárrenme'. Bueno, nosotros respondimos a ese llamado".
Con esas palabras, el secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. Pete Hegseth, presumió de la captura de Maduro durante una visita a Venezuela en la que se reunió con la presidenta interina, Delcy Rodríguez, para firmar un acuerdo de cooperación militar.
Durante un discurso pronunciado en la sede de la Embajada de EE.UU. Hegseth describió la captura de Maduro como "la operación militar más sofisticada en la historia de América Latina" y aseguró que el 3 de enero -cuando fue ejecutada- pasará a la historia de Venezuela como "un día de liberación".
"Es un gran honor ser el primer secretario de Guerra en este siglo en pisar Venezuela. El peso de este momento no se me escapa. Hace apenas un año, mi presencia aquí, nuestra presencia aquí habría sido considerada imposible, casi inimaginable", dijo.
Hegseth afirmó que eso había sido posible gracias al mandatario estadounidense, Donald Trump.
"Tuvo el coraje para hacer lo que ningún presidente anterior estuvo dispuesto a hacer: defender la patria estadounidense con acciones, no solo con palabras. Y porque él lo hizo hace casi un año, los mejores y más valientes guerreros estadounidenses solucionaron un problema de 27 años de antigüedad para este hemisferio en cuestión de horas", apuntó.
"El resultado fue, como había predicho Maduro, 'no guerra, sí paz'. Paz a través de la fuerza para llevar a narcoterroristas hasta la justicia y empezar un nuevo capítulo para EE.UU., para Venezuela, para los militares venezolanos y para el hemisferio occidental", agregó luego.
Cooperación militar
La visita del jefe del Pentágono a Caracas se produjo en el contexto de una gira por países de América Latina.
Antes de su discurso en la sede diplomática, Hegseth acudió al Palacio de Miraflores, sede del Poder Ejecutivo, donde firmó con Delcy Rodríguez un acuerdo de cooperación militar entre el Pentágono y las Fuerzas Armadas de Venezuela.
El alto funcionario estadounidense dijo que se trata del "restablecimiento" de lazos militares entre ambos países.
Aunque no se ofrecieron muchos detalles, la prensa oficial en Venezuela aseguró que se trata de un acuerdo que "respetará la independencia y la soberanía nacional".
Hegseth calificó el pacto como "un restablecimiento de nuestra alianza de defensa" y afirmó que traía los saludos del presidente Trump, quien esperaba con interés trabajar juntos. "No solo en el ámbito militar contra los narcoterroristas y las organizaciones criminales", dijo, "sino también en el económico, aprovechando las extraordinarias capacidades de recursos de Venezuela".
Por su parte, Delcy Rodríguez elogió lo que describió como la "madurez política" que había permitido a estos dos antiguos enemigos reconstruir sus relaciones de trabajo. El acuerdo con el Pentágono "fortalecerá la capacidad de la Fuerza Armada Nacional Bolivariana", afirmó, al proporcionar "equipamiento operativo" y acceso a nuevas tecnologías.
El objetivo de este último acuerdo firmado con Washington, añadió, es "hacer frente a amenazas comunes".
Desde la captura de Maduro en enero, Estados Unidos asumió una suerte de tutela sobre Venezuela que incluye el control sobre la venta del petróleo de ese país. Además, respaldó la permanencia de Delcy Rodríguez en el poder como presidenta interina.

title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
rawText:
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.
Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.
The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.
Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.
In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.
If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).
According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.
In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.
“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.
The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

title: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
rawText:
NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
- Date:
- November 17, 2026
- Source:
- NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
- Summary:
- NASA has successfully tested Mars helicopter rotor blades at supersonic speeds, boosting potential lift by 30% and overcoming a major obstacle to more powerful aircraft on the Red Planet. The breakthrough could enable next-generation helicopters to carry heavier scientific equipment, fly farther, and explore places beyond the reach of traditional rovers.
- Share:
NASA is pushing the limits of helicopter flight on Mars, testing rotor blades at speeds once considered too risky. The faster these blades spin, the more lift they can generate, potentially allowing future aircraft to carry heavier scientific instruments and travel greater distances across the Red Planet.
During tests conducted in March at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, engineers successfully pushed the tips of experimental Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound without causing them to break apart. The experiments took place inside a specialized chamber designed to reproduce the harsh atmospheric conditions on Mars. Results from 137 test runs could help engineers develop a new generation of more powerful aircraft capable of carrying scientific equipment.
"NASA had a great run with the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, but we are asking these next-generation aircraft to do even more at the Red Planet," said Al Chen, Mars Exploration Program manager at JPL. "That's not an easy ask. While everything about Mars is hard, flying there is just about the hardest thing you can do. That's because its atmosphere is so incredibly thin that it is hard to generate lift, and yet Mars has significant gravity."
Ingenuity made history on April 19, 2021, when it became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another world. However, it was designed primarily to demonstrate that flight on Mars was possible, not to transport scientific instruments. NASA now hopes to go much further. Its recently announced SkyFall project, along with other potential future aircraft, could carry sensors and scientific instruments to investigate Mars from the air. Flying at low altitudes would provide valuable information to support future robotic and human missions.
Why Flying on Mars Requires Extreme Rotor Speeds
Helicopters generate more thrust by spinning their rotors faster or using blades with a larger diameter. That basic principle applies on Earth and Mars, but the Red Planet presents a much greater engineering challenge.
Mars has an atmosphere only about 1% as dense as Earth's, leaving helicopter blades with far fewer air molecules to push against. To produce enough lift, engineers must operate rotors at exceptionally high speeds, bringing their tips close to the speed of sound. Small rotors on Earth can also spin thousands of times per minute, but the denser atmosphere makes it unnecessary to push their tips toward supersonic speeds to generate substantial lift.
During Ingenuity's 72 flights on Mars, its engineers limited the helicopter's composite-skinned foam rotors to 2,700 revolutions per minute. This restriction served two important purposes. It kept the blades away from the complex and potentially unpredictable conditions near the sound barrier, and it provided a safety margin in case sudden winds (from a dust devil, for instance) caused the blade tips to move faster relative to the surrounding air.
"If Chuck Yeager were here, he'd tell you things can get squirrely around Mach 1," said JPL's Jaakko Karras, the rotor test lead. "With that in mind, we planned Ingenuity's flights to keep the rotor blade tips at Mach 0.7 with no wind so that if we encountered a Martian headwind while in flight, the rotor tips wouldn't go supersonic. But we want more performance from our next-gen Mars aircraft. We needed to know that our rotors could go faster safely."

title: Cómo fue el sofisticado ataque con el que Ucrania destruyó parte del preciado puente de Crimea de Putin (y qué consecuencias tendrá)
rawText:
Cómo fue el sofisticado ataque con el que Ucrania destruyó parte del preciado puente de Crimea de Putin (y qué consecuencias tendrá)
  - Autor, Laura Gozzi
  - Título del autor, BBC News
  - Autor, Ilya Abishev
  - Título del autor, Corresponsal de Defensa de BBC en Rusia
  - Autor, Richard Irvine-Brown
  - Título del autor, BBC Verify
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 6 min
El puente de Crimea, que atraviesa el estrecho de Kerch sobre el mar Negro, ha sido un símbolo desde que se acabó su construcción.
Para Rusia, es un proyecto prestigioso que consolida su reivindicación sobre el territorio ucraniano soberano. Para Ucrania, una infraestructura detestada, emblemática de la ocupación de la península de Crimea por parte de Moscú.
Una sección clave del puente de doble arco y 19 kilómetros de longitud yace ahora en el fondo del mar, derribada por el armamento ucraniano de largo alcance en una operación de siete fases que culminó en un dramático derrumbe.
El portavoz del Kremlin, Dmitri Peskov, ha declarado que el puente "será reconstruido y quedará incluso mejor que antes".
Pero ocho años después de su inauguración, el puente se ha convertido en una prueba material de la capacidad de Kyiv para atravesar las defensas militares de Moscú y alcanzar incluso sus estructuras más preciadas y protegidas.
Una operación en 7 etapas
El ataque contra el estratégico puente de Crimea se llevó a cabo de forma gradual para atravesar distintas capas de defensa, según informó Kyiv este martes.
Durante varias semanas, el Servicio de Seguridad de Ucrania y su Estado Mayor destruyeron gradualmente sistemas de defensa aérea, radares, sistemas de guerra electrónica y otros objetivos designados, dijo el presidente Volodymyr Zelensky.
El 16 de noviembre ya se había registrado un incidente importante cuando varios drones impactaron el puente durante la noche. El tráfico se interrumpió y luego se reanudó. Aunque el arco que se alza sobre la calzada resultó visiblemente dañado, la estructura no colapsó.
Pero ese golpe resultó ser solo la penúltima etapa de un ataque complejo.
En la madrugada del 17 de noviembre, los ataques finales dieron el golpe definitivo a la ya debilitada estructura del arco.
Un vídeo verificado –grabado desde una cámara a bordo de un misil Flamingo de fabricación ucraniana– muestra al arma acercándose al tramo principal del puente y dirigiéndose hacia los arcos de acero, con la grabación congelándose justo antes del impacto.
Según Justin Bronk, experto en municiones del Royal United Services Institute, el misil Flamingo podría haber sido modificado para ser controlado a la distancia, lo que mejoró su precisión lo suficiente como para alcanzar los pilares del puente.
Bronk añadió que la "ojiva muy pesada" del misil lo hacía "más adecuado" para atacar los tramos y soportes de hormigón armado del puente.
Más tarde, Zelensky confirmó que en el ataque se utilizaron varios tipos de misiles y drones, lo que llevó al colapso del enorme arco, una estructura de unos 227 metros de longitud y un peso de miles de toneladas.
Las imágenes diurnas captadas desde la costa norte de Crimea muestran que un tramo de aproximadamente 200 metros de la carretera se desplomó y fue arrastrado al mar
Se trata claramente de un daño crítico para el puente. Lejos de ser un mero elemento decorativo, el arco desempeñaba una función estructural. Distribuía las cargas, sostenía el tramo principal y contribuía a garantizar la estabilidad de toda la estructura.
El arco paralelo que sostiene el tramo ferroviario se ha mantenido en pie, aunque es posible que también haya sufrido daños. En un primer momento, se suspendió todo el tráfico en el puente, aunque después permitieron que los trenes reanudaran su circulación.
Sin embargo, los daños en el tramo principal del puente son "catastróficos", declaró a BBC Verify Colin Capriani, ingeniero estructural de la Universidad de Monash en Melbourne, Australia.

title: Magnificent Wales beat New Zealand for first time since 1953
rawText:
Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo
- Published
Nations Championship
Wales (21) 35
Tries: T Williams, Lake, Griffin, James, Rees-Zammit Cons: Costelow 5
New Zealand (21) 28
Tries: Ratima, Sititi, Fineanganofo, Lakai Cons: Mo'unga 4.
Wales celebrated a first victory against New Zealand in 73 years with a brilliant performance to spark astonishing scenes in Cardiff.
Steve Tandy's unfancied side lifted a nation as they broke a 34-match losing sequence against the All Blacks that stretched back to 1953.
In a nine-try Nations Championship thriller at the Principality Stadium, Wales led 14-0, 21-7 and 35-21 before they held off New Zealand with a wonderful defensive display in the final quarter, led by flankers James Botham and Jac Morgan and lock Dafydd Jenkins.
The home side produced a stunning start with tries from inspirational scrum-half Tomos Williams and captain Dewi Lake inside the first six minutes.
Prop Archie Griffin also added a first-half try, but New Zealand responded with scores from scrum-half Cortez Ratima, number eight Wallace Sititi and wing Fehi Fineanganofo to level the score 21-21 at half-time.
Wales centre Eddie James and wing Louis Rees-Zammit scored early second-half tries before New Zealand flanker Peter Lakai pulled one back.
The remarkable Wales defence followed as they held up the All Blacks three times over the line to stop New Zealand scoring, to evoke wild celebrations.
- Wales believed they could create history - Lake 
  - Published24 minutes ago
- All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett 
  - Published36 minutes ago
Good things come to those who wait
Wales had won the first three games in this fixture in 1905, 1935 and 1953 but have had to wait more than seven decades for the next.
In 1953 the New Zealand dollar did not exist, Cardiff was not the capital city of Wales and tries were only worth three points.
Sections of the New Zealand media had belittled Welsh rugby before the game, while some bookmakers offered odds of 20-1 for a Wales victory.
Legends such as Sir Gareth Edwards, Alun Wyn Jones, Shane Williams, JPR Williams, Barry John and Phil Bennett had never enjoyed success against New Zealand in a Welsh jersey.
Now Tandy's class of 2026 have written their own chapter in Welsh rugby's history.
The 55,152 was the lowest crowd in the 14 matches between Wales and New Zealand at the Principality Stadium. The fans who stayed away will regret it because it was a day to say "I was there".
Welsh rugby has been in the doldrums for so long, on and off the field, but will hope this famous victory can help galvanise the nation.
This was one of the finest performances in Welsh rugby history and a world apart from the display in the 28-21 win against Japan last weekend.
New Zealand might regret failing to take advantage of France's victory against South Africa on Friday night but they still leapfrog the Springboks to top the southern section with one weekend of regular matches remaining.
Fast start for Wales as hosts dare to dream
Wales made four changes to the side that beat Japan, with Taine Basham making his first Test start in four years by replacing injured number eight Aaron Wainwright.
Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb was preferred to Josh Adams, who scored two tries against Japan, while lock Adam Beard and flanker Botham came in for Ben Carter and Alex Mann.
New Zealand made eight starting swaps from the team that beat Scotland 43-21, with full-back Beauden Barrett handed the Test captaincy for the first time in his 149th international.
New Zealand's haka was the usual piece of theatre as the All Blacks were lit up by a spotlight and Wales in red.
The hosts reacted quickest from the start with prop Nicky Smith winning a turnover before an excellent long pass from Williams released Rees-Zammit.
The wing chipped ahead and Williams, who New Zealand coach Dave Rennie had highlighted as a pre-match dangerman, pounced for the try.

title: The Jensen Huang Scandal Has Shocked Even Scandal-Prone Silicon Valley
rawText:
Supported by
News analysis
Silicon Valley Is Used to Scandal. This One Upped the Ante.
As Jensen Huang abruptly departs, the tech community grapples with an eternal question: Why do the smartest and most successful men so often act so stupidly?
Artificial intelligence promises transcendence. We will ditch our tired and inefficient bodies, say farewell to tedious work and trips to the grocery store. The computer will tend to all human needs and solve all human problems.
Well, that was the idea. A.I. was supposed to achieve a new level of reality this month with the public sale of shares of Anthropic, one of the two start-ups that have created and defined this young industry. A trillion-dollar company will be born, yielding billionaires galore.
A.I. is the biggest Silicon Valley story ever. But last Sunday it was suddenly pushed aside when the chief executive of the company whose chips are literally powering this intelligence revolution confessed to cheating on his wife with a woman, Alice Huang, who U.S. officials believe was spying for China. By Thursday morning he had resigned, something few thought possible just days earlier.
The scandal that took down Nvidia chief Jensen Huang is full of implications for national security and the global A.I. boom. Mr. Huang ranked among Mark Zuckerberg, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Bill Gates as tech leaders who were considered by the world to be inseparable from the companies they built.
In Silicon Valley, people were mostly just stunned by the news. Those who have been around for a long time, and seen the stretch of territory south of San Francisco evolve from hardware manufacturing to software development to the dot-com frenzy and now the A.I. boom, said they had never seen anything like it.
Tech veterans have witnessed amazing ascensions and equally abrupt falls. They have seen abundant arrogance. Fortunes made and fortunes lost in an instant. But there’s something that stands out this time: Transcendence was never supposed to be tawdry.

title: Teen prodigy, Netflix star, prisoner: the story of Hong Kong dissident Joshua Wong – podcast

He has been leading protests since he was 14. Joshua Wong has been on the cover of Time magazine, the focus of a Netflix documentary and an icon for Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement.

title: Here’s the latest.
rawText:
Nvidia Updates: Huang’s Resignation Reverberates Through A.I. Industry
Jensen Huang had been entangled with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy and with an executive who reported to him. Lawmakers on Capitol Hill called for investigations into whether national security had been compromised.
Latest
The abrupt resignation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Thursday morning after revelations that he had extramarital affairs with two women sent shock waves through the A.I. industry and spurred calls on Capitol Hill for investigations into whether U.S. security had been compromised.
Mr. Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant, stepped down after Nvidia’s board started an inquiry into allegations that he had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China, as well as with an executive who reported to him.
It was the stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of artificial intelligence projects.
Mr. Huang’s exit is expected to have widespread ripple effects. One question is what will happen to Nvidia’s supply chain in Asia, where Mr. Huang created an intricate web of overlapping suppliers, all held together with his personal relationships.
It also touched the White House, where Mr. Huang long had a firm ally in President Trump. The president defended Mr. Huang all week and praised him again on Thursday for doing a “fantastic job”; Mr. Trump then recommended that Tim Cook, the former Apple chief executive, take the helm at Nvidia.
A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang, 63, had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang. The Times also reported that Mr. Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action.
U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped to smuggle restricted chips into China. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment; China has rejected the espionage claims and called the smuggling allegations “smears.”
On Capitol Hill, Democrats called for an investigation into whether Mr. Huang had compromised U.S. national security. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, said the Trump administration also “must answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.”
Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, said on Thursday that he anticipated Mr. Huang’s resignation would not keep Congress from conducting hearings on his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. “It would make sense because of the nature of the association,” he said.
Here’s what else to know:
- Nvidia’s board: The board did not mention Mr. Huang’s conduct in its statement announcing his resignation. Instead, it thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent replacement is carried out, it said.
- Another affair: Mr. Huang had a second extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. He is the latest member to join a growing club of chief executives brought down by affairs.
- A long-term strategy: China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people. Although the use of seduction in espionage is not unique to China, the country’s use of it differs in the amount of time it is willing to invest. Read more ›

title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
rawText:
China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.
The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.
Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”
China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.
Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.
Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.
“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.
“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”
It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.
After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.
China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.
Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.
That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.
India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.
The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.

title: Microsoft’s Outlook email hit by new outage
rawText:
Microsoft said its Outlook email service is currently experiencing an outage, preventing users from accessing their inboxes.
The issue was initially flagged as affecting the U.S. and the Americas, and later expanded to affect “any region.”
Microsoft hasn’t given a specific cause, but said that it was providing updates in its admin center, which wasn’t reachable at the time of publication. In a post on X for users who can’t access the admin center, Microsoft said some of its infrastructure was experiencing “elevated load,” and that it was “redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load.”
The company’s last major incident was in September, when a days-long outage hit Microsoft 365, its online productivity suite that includes Outlook. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service.
It’s unclear to what extent the outage extends to other services. TechCrunch will reach out to Microsoft for comment, as soon as our email service has resumed.
